payload.title: Greek Orthodox Wedding Requirements and Ceremony Explained
payload.audience: Couples in their 30s interested in destination weddings and luxury experiences, AUD 150k+ budget
payload.reader: An Australian couple in their 30s with a budget of AUD 150k or more, at least one of them Greek Orthodox or from a Greek-Australian family (often with parents contributing and holding firm views), who want an Orthodox ceremony, possibly in Greece. They need to know, before they book anything, whether the Church will marry them (especially if one partner is not Orthodox), which dates are ruled out, what papers the Church and the State each need, how the marriage is recognised back in Australia, and what actually happens in the service, so they can talk to their priest and family with confidence and then plan the celebration around it.
payload.goal: Speak with a Wedded Advisor: request a Wedded Concierge consultation at /wonderland-concierge so an advisor can plan the venue, travel, vendors and guest stays around the ceremony the couple's priest confirms (the church and legal paperwork stays with the couple, their priest and the authorities).
payload.angle: Page-one results for 'greek orthodox wedding' are mostly symbolism listicles or single-parish pages; few put the Church's own rules, the dates it does not marry, the two-track paperwork (church then civil registration) and the full service order in one place. This guide does, and it is honest about whose rules are whose: eligibility, sponsor and calendar rules are given as the named church jurisdiction states them (for example 'the Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of America's guidelines say'), never as universal law, and every section sends the couple to their own parish priest for the final word. It separates what the Church requires from what Greek and Australian civil law requires, as at November 2026, and walks through the service step by step, giving meanings only where a church source gives them. It ends with what is different when the ceremony is in Greece (a venue chapel versus a parish church, as venues state them) and a short list of questions to ask about music, photography, dress and timing.
must_include: Intro with a direct answer in the first 100 words: a Greek Orthodox wedding is a sacrament with its own service and its own rules on who can marry and when; check eligibility and dates with your parish priest before booking a venue. Link /expert-advice/greek-wedding-traditions here (anchor about Greek wedding traditions and the customs around the service).

Exactly 4 one-sentence Key takeaways (eligibility depends on the jurisdiction and your priest; some dates and periods are closed to weddings; church and civil paperwork are separate tracks; the crowning is the heart of the service).

Who can marry in the Orthodox Church: Orthodox partner; non-Orthodox Christian partner (baptised in the name of the Trinity, if the source says so); interfaith (non-Christian partner); sponsor (koumbaros/koumbara) rules. Each rule attributed to the named jurisdiction whose guidelines state it, e.g. 'the Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of America's guidelines say', and followed by 'ask your parish priest'. If a jurisdiction is silent on a point, say so plainly rather than fill the gap.

When weddings are not held: only the periods and days a church source lists (for example fasting periods and specific feast days), attributed to that jurisdiction, with 'confirm the calendar with your priest for your year'. No invented dates.

Documents and the Metropolis licence: the church documents a source lists (for example baptism certificates, the sponsor's eligibility, a church licence or permit from the local Metropolis for a wedding in Greece) as the source states them. Then civil registration in Greece and recognition in Australia, as at November 2026, dated once: Greek civil registration of a religious marriage and the Australian side (Smartraveller, Australian Embassy Athens, apostille or Certificate of No Impediment only as official sources state). Where a step or fee is not stated, write 'check with the Metropolis, the municipality and the embassy, including any fees'.

The ceremony step by step, in order: betrothal and rings; candles; joining of hands; crowning with the stefana; readings (Epistle and Gospel); common cup; Dance of Isaiah; removing the crowns and the closing blessing. Meanings only where a church source gives them; otherwise describe what happens with 'usually'. Consistent with, but not copied from, the Greek traditions final (no vows, the koumbaros exchanges rings and crowns).

Planning one in Greece: venue chapel versus parish church only as venues state them (example venue names only, at most 2 to 3, linked to the sister guides rather than described); questions to ask the priest and venue on music, photography and video, dress and covered shoulders, ceremony timing and length, language of the service, and guest numbers inside the church. This section carries the ONLY Advisor line in the body (brand-facts claims only, framed around venue, travel, vendors and guests, never paperwork), plus a link to /wonderland-concierge. Links: /destination-weddings/santorini-wedding, /destination-weddings/mykonos-wedding, /destination-weddings/rhodes-wedding-venues, /destination-weddings/greece-wedding-venues.

FAQ (4 to 6): Can a non-Orthodox partner marry in a Greek Orthodox church? Do we need a koumbaros, and who can be one? Are there vows in a Greek Orthodox wedding? Is a church wedding in Greece legally recognised in Australia? When can't you have a Greek Orthodox wedding? How long is the service (only if a church source gives it, else drop)?

Close: the one Advisor line from brand-facts.md (never the definition line or its closing phrase). The Greek Orthodox Archdiocese of Australia is named only in an 'ask your parish priest' line (its page is not read, so nothing is attributed to it). Links: /expert-advice/greek-wedding-traditions (both ways), /destination-weddings/greece-wedding-venues, /wonderland-concierge (anchor names 'Wedded Concierge'), /magazine as the magnet. UTMs utm_source=blog&utm_medium=content&utm_campaign=greek-orthodox-wedding&utm_content=primary|secondary|magnet|closing on /wonderland-concierge and /magazine only.
avoid: Any price, fee, donation, stole fee or amount; 'free'; transfers, drive or flight times.
Any position on same-sex marriage, in the church or civil sections.
Anything that implies the Wedded Advisor or Wedded Concierge helps with legal, church or religious paperwork, licences, sponsors or priests.
Stating any church rule as universal or as the Archdiocese of Australia's; rules without a named jurisdiction; filling gaps a church source does not cover.
Meanings or symbolism not given by a church source; folklore presented as church teaching (folklore belongs to the Greek traditions guide).
Restating the Greek traditions guide's customs (krevati, koufeta, shoe, dances at the reception) beyond a one-line link; that guide keeps 'greek wedding traditions'.
Venue descriptions beyond what the sister venue guides state; venue contact or business details; vendor names.

Research talk in copy ('we could not confirm', 'on its own site'); per-line source credits; hedge stacking; linking a source more than once. Naming the church jurisdiction for its own rules is allowed.
Competitor wedding sites, directories, planner blogs or Wikipedia as sources; competitor wording or images.

Wedded Privileges; Advisor claims beyond brand-facts.md; more than one Advisor line in the body besides the close; the Advisor definition line and the phrase 'last dance'; 'Wonderland Concierge' as anchor text.
Clichés (fairytale, dream day, breathtaking), exclamation marks, keywords pasted in headings, em dashes, US spelling.
AI images of any church, venue, destination or wedding; images other than placeholders with consent and parish photography notes.
